blocks.text: In 1801 Thomas Young used this experiment to show the wave nature of light. A beam of light falls on a pair of parallel slits at right angles to the beam. Light diffracts and spreads outward from each slit, and the light from the two slits overlaps on a screen, forming an interference pattern of bright and dark bands called fringes. The two sources must be coherent, with a constant phase difference and the same wavelength; today this is easily achieved by passing one laser beam through the two slits (Fig 15.8).

blocks.alt: On the left, three vertical wavefronts crossed by four horizontal pink rays labelled rays, arriving at a barrier with two slits S1 and S2. Beyond the barrier, circular wavefronts spread out from each slit and cross each other on the way to a screen on the right.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.8: Double slit arrangement (printed in the book as Fig. 15.9; original drawing after the textbook's figure).

items: Point A, directly opposite the midpoint of the slits: the two rays travel equal distances, so the path difference is zero. Leaving the slits in phase, they arrive in phase and interfere constructively: a bright fringe.

Point B, the middle of the first dark fringe: the light from slit 1 travels slightly further, and the path difference is half a wavelength. The rays arrive in antiphase (180 degrees) and interfere destructively.
Point C, the middle of the next bright fringe: the path difference is a whole wavelength, so the rays arrive in phase and interfere constructively.

blocks.alt: Three parts, each with slits S1 and S2 a distance d apart and a screen at distance L, with wavy rays from both slits. (a) The rays meet at the centre of the screen: bright (constructive interference). (b) The rays meet higher up; the lower ray travels an extra distance of half a wavelength, shown by a grey triangle: dark (destructive interference). (c) Higher still, extra distance one wavelength: bright. The angle theta is marked.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.9: (a) for theta = 0, central bright region; (b) first dark region; (c) first order bright region (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.9, whose captions for (b) and (c) are swapped).

blocks.text: To simplify the analysis, assume the distance L from the slits to the screen is so large compared with the slit separation d that the lines from S1 and S2 to a point P are nearly parallel. This is usually so for light: the slit separation is a fraction of a millimetre to a few millimetres, while the screen is a metre or more away. The path difference is then r2 - r1 = d sin(theta) (15.1), where theta is the angle between the line from the slits to P and the normal to the plane of the slits.

Constructive interference (reinforcement) occurs where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, so bright regions occur at angles theta for which d sin(theta) = m lambda, with m = 0, 1, 2, 3, ... (15.2). Destructive interference (cancellation), forming dark regions, occurs where the path difference is a half-integer number of wavelengths: d sin(theta) = (m + 1/2) lambda. The pattern is a succession of bright and dark bands parallel to the slits.

blocks.alt: Two slits in a grey barrier, S2 above and S1 below, a distance d apart, and a screen at distance L on the right. Blue rays r2 and r1 go from the slits to a point P on the screen at height y below the centre line. The angle theta is marked between the centre line and the ray, and again at the slits, where a short extra length of the S2 ray is labelled d sin theta.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.10: Schematic double slit arrangement (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.10).

blocks.text: Positions of the fringes: let ym be the distance from the centre of the pattern (theta = 0) to the centre of the mth bright band, and theta_m the corresponding angle. Then ym = L tan(theta_m) (15.3). In such experiments ym is much smaller than L, so theta_m is very small and sin(theta_m) is approximately tan(theta_m); thus ym = L sin(theta_m) (15.4). Using d sin(theta_m) = m lambda, the position of the mth bright band is ym = m L lambda / d (15.5), and the distance between the centres of neighbouring bright (or dark) fringes is dy = L lambda / d (15.6).

The fringe spacing is inversely proportional to the slit separation d: the closer the slits, the more the pattern spreads out. These results apply to any type of wave, provided the resultant wave from two coherent sources is detected at a point far away compared with d.
